papers.title: LIFE-seq: longitudinal spatial transcriptomics of living tissue
papers.summary: LIFE-seq appears to be a new method for performing spatial transcriptomics on living tissue over time, rather than on fixed snapshots. This would allow researchers to track gene expression changes in the same tissue sample across multiple time points. Such longitudinal spatial data could reveal dynamic processes that static spatial transcriptomics methods miss.
papers.why: Longitudinal spatial transcriptomics in living tissue could enable tracking of dynamic autophagy and mitophagy gene expression changes in neurons and interneurons over time within their spatial brain context, rather than relying on fixed time-point snapshots.
papers.figure: Figure showing the experimental workflow/timeline comparing longitudinal live-tissue transcriptomic capture versus traditional single-timepoint spatial transcriptomics.

papers.title: Decoder-FFPE-seq enables sensitive, genome-wide spatial transcriptomics of archival tissues at single-cell resolution.
papers.summary: This paper introduces Decoder-FFPE-seq, a new method for performing spatial transcriptomics on archival formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples. The technique allows researchers to measure gene expression across the whole genome at single-cell resolution while preserving spatial information within the tissue. This means scientists can now retrospectively study gene expression patterns in large banks of preserved clinical or historical tissue samples with high sensitivity.
papers.why: This method could allow retrospective spatial transcriptomic analysis of archival human or animal brain tissue, potentially enabling studies of interneuron and perineuronal net gene expression in banked FFPE brain samples that would otherwise be inaccessible to fresh-tissue spatial methods.
papers.figure: A figure showing a comparison of gene detection sensitivity and spatial resolution between Decoder-FFPE-seq and conventional spatial transcriptomics methods on matched FFPE tissue sections.

papers.title: spOT-NMF: gene expression deconvolution via optimal transport with proximity-aware niche mapping for spatial transcriptomics.
papers.summary: spOT-NMF is a computational method that uses optimal transport theory combined with non-negative matrix factorization to deconvolve spatial transcriptomics data, estimating cell-type or gene expression contributions at each spatial spot. The 'proximity-aware niche mapping' component incorporates spatial distances between spots to better model local tissue microenvironments or niches. This approach aims to improve the accuracy of spatial deconvolution compared to methods that ignore spatial context.
papers.why: This tool could help deconvolve spatial transcriptomics data to resolve interneuron subtypes and their spatial niches relative to perineuronal nets, improving analysis of cell-type-specific mitophagy signals in complex brain tissue.
papers.figure: A figure showing the spatial niche mapping output overlaid on tissue architecture, illustrating how proximity-aware deconvolution resolves cell-type boundaries compared to standard methods.

papers.title: Edaravone Dexborneol via SLC33A1 Modulates Microglial Lipid Droplet Homeostasis to Suppress Neuronal Necroptosis in Acute Ischemic Stroke.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the drug Edaravone Dexborneol affects microglia, the brain's immune cells, during acute ischemic stroke. It finds that the drug works through a protein called SLC33A1 to regulate lipid droplets inside microglia, which helps maintain their normal function. By controlling this lipid droplet balance, the drug reduces a form of programmed cell death (necroptosis) in neurons, potentially limiting stroke damage.
papers.why: While focused on stroke and microglia rather than autophagy/mitophagy in interneurons, the paper's methods linking microglial lipid metabolism to neuronal cell death pathways could inform complementary analyses of organelle and lipid dynamics in spatial omics datasets.
papers.figure: A figure showing lipid droplet quantification in microglia alongside neuronal necroptosis markers (e.g., pMLKL) under SLC33A1 modulation.

papers.title: Urolithin A ameliorates experimental autoimmune myasthenia gravisin association with mitochondrial quality control-related and inflammasome signaling changes.
papers.summary: This study tests Urolithin A, a natural compound known to boost mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria), in a mouse model of autoimmune myasthenia gravis, a disease where the immune system attacks neuromuscular junctions. The researchers found that Urolithin A treatment improved disease symptoms and was linked to changes in mitochondrial quality control pathways and inflammasome signaling, which is part of the innate immune response. This suggests the compound's benefits may come from both cleaning up damaged mitochondria and reducing inflammation.
papers.why: Although this paper focuses on neuromuscular junctions rather than brain interneurons, it provides relevant mechanistic insight into how Urolithin A modulates mitophagy and inflammasome signaling, which could inform approaches to studying mitochondrial quality control in neuronal health.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitophagy marker expression (e.g., PINK1/Parkin pathway) alongside inflammasome activation markers (e.g., NLRP3) in treated versus untreated disease model tissue.

papers.title: Targeting Mitochondrial Quality Control with Nanomedicine for Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury: A Critical Review of Preclinical Strategies.
papers.summary: This review examines preclinical research on using nanomedicine-based approaches to target mitochondrial quality control pathways, such as mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis, to protect against ischemia-reperfusion injury. It covers how nanoparticles can be engineered to deliver drugs specifically to damaged mitochondria, enhancing clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria or supporting healthy ones. The review critically evaluates various nanocarrier strategies tested in animal or cell models, discussing their mechanisms, efficacy, and translational challenges.
papers.why: Although focused on ischemia-reperfusion rather than neurons directly, this review could offer useful insights into mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy-targeting nanotechnology that may inspire therapeutic or imaging strategies relevant to neuronal mitophagy research.

papers.title: Mitochondrial LONP1: Linking structure and function to context‑dependent roles in disease (Review).
papers.summary: This review focuses on LONP1, a mitochondrial protease that helps degrade damaged proteins and maintain mitochondrial quality control. It discusses how LONP1's structure relates to its function, and how its activity can have different, context-dependent effects in various diseases. The paper synthesizes current understanding of LONP1 biology without presenting new experimental data.
papers.why: LONP1-mediated mitochondrial quality control is mechanistically upstream of mitophagy regulation in neurons, making this structural/functional context directly relevant to understanding mitochondrial turnover in brain cells.
papers.figure: A structural diagram showing LONP1's domain architecture and its proteolytic/chaperone functions in mitochondrial protein quality control.

papers.title: Gene therapy and mitochondrial transplantation for mitochondrial dysfunction in aging.
papers.summary: This paper reviews emerging strategies to address mitochondrial dysfunction associated with aging, focusing on two approaches: gene therapy targeting mitochondrial genes or pathways, and mitochondrial transplantation where healthy mitochondria are directly introduced into cells or tissues. These methods aim to restore cellular energy production and reduce oxidative damage that accumulates with age. The abstract suggests these interventions could potentially reverse or mitigate age-related decline in mitochondrial function across various tissues.
papers.why: Since mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy are central to neuronal aging and the PhD project's focus on mitochondrial quality control in brain cells, understanding therapeutic strategies to restore mitochondrial health could inform interpretations of spatial omics data on mitochondrial states in interneurons.
